query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The combination of low density, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance in lightweight high-entropy alloys can be achieved through the formation of a stable simple solid solution phase, which is facilitated by the high configurational entropy of these alloys.
generation.conditions: aerospace and rail-transport operating conditions, including high temperatures and corrosive environments
generation.mechanism: high configurational entropy facilitating the formation of a stable simple solid solution phase
generation.predicted_outcome: a 20% increase in strength-to-weight ratio and a 30% improvement in corrosion resistance compared to traditional alloys
generation.boundary: alloys with a configurational entropy below a certain threshold
generation.uncertainty: the exact relationship between configurational entropy and the formation of a stable simple solid solution phase is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: controlled comparison of the properties of lightweight high-entropy alloys with different configurational entropies
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the strength-to-weight ratio and corrosion resistance of the alloys with higher configurational entropy are not significantly improved compared to those with lower configurational entropy, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: This study provides new perspectives and a new understanding of the oxidation and corrosion behaviors of high-entropy alloys, revealing their outstanding performance during the oxidation process. With the development of materials science, high-entropy alloys, as a novel material, possess great potential in industrial applications due to their superior mechanical properties, high-temperature resistance, and corrosion resistance. In the future, with continuous research, it is expected that high-entropy alloys will be widely applied in various fields such as aerospace, energy, chemical engineering, and automotive manufacturing. Especially in high-temperature, high-pressure, and extreme environments, they are expected to become important structural and functional materials.

Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), firstly proposed in 2004, have attracted extensive attention due to their outstanding mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, irradiation resistance and thermal stability [,,,,]. HEAs are generally composed of at least five kinds of elements with an atomic percentage between 5% and 35% in equal mole or near equal mole ratios [,]. Differing from conventional alloys, HEAs tend to form simple solid solution structures, such as face-centered cubic (FCC), body-centered cubic (BCC) and close-packed hexagonal (HCP), rather than intermetallic compounds or amorphous phases due to their higher mix entropy [,,,]. However, the existing HEAs also contain several intermetallic compounds, which can strengthen the mechanical properties [,]. With the urgent demand for structural materials for application in high-temperature conditions, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), generally composed of refractory elements, were proposed in 2010 [].
